formula_sheet.expr: First law: energy is converted, not created or destroyed; Second law: every transfer degrades some energy to heat
formula_sheet.note: Hence energy flow is unidirectional and cannot be recycled, unlike nutrients

diagrams.title: Trophic levels in an ecosystem (NCERT Fig. 12.1 style)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw four boxes or bars stacked vertically. Bottom: 'Producers (green plants), first trophic level'. Above it: 'Primary consumers (herbivores), second trophic level'. Then 'Secondary consumers (primary carnivores), third trophic level' and at the top 'Tertiary consumers (secondary carnivores), fourth trophic level'. Put a named example beside each (grass, grasshopper or goat, frog or snake, hawk or man) and upward arrows between the boxes for the direction of energy. Label the axis 'trophic level' and title it. The four levels correctly named with their alternative names (herbivore, primary carnivore, secondary carnivore) earn the marks.

diagrams.title: Energy flow through an ecosystem (NCERT Fig. 12.2 style)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the sun at the far left with an arrow labelled 'solar radiation (less than 50 per cent is PAR; plants capture 2 to 10 per cent of PAR)' into a box 'Producers'. Continue in a line: Producers → Primary consumers → Secondary consumers → Tertiary consumers, each arrow labelled with roughly 10 per cent of the previous value (for example 10,000, 1,000, 100, 10). From every box draw a downward arrow into a single wide box at the bottom labelled 'Decomposers (detritus food chain)'. From every box, including the decomposers, draw a wavy arrow going out labelled 'heat loss (respiration)'. Add the caption 'unidirectional flow of energy'. The examiner checks for the sun, the four trophic levels, the decomposers receiving from all levels, and heat lost at every step.

diagrams.title: Grazing food chain and detritus food chain and their connection
diagrams.how_to_draw: On the left write the grazing chain vertically: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk (or NCERT's Grass → Goat → Man). On the right write the detritus chain: Dead organic matter (detritus) → Decomposers (fungi, bacteria) → Detritivores (earthworm) → their predators. Draw arrows from every organism in the grazing chain to 'detritus' (death, faeces, fallen leaves) and an arrow from earthworm to a bird in the grazing chain, labelled 'DFC organisms are prey to GFC animals'. Add 'omnivores such as crow and cockroach feed at both'. Title it 'Interconnection of GFC and DFC forms a food web'.

diagrams.title: Pyramid of numbers in a grassland (upright)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw four horizontal bars centred on a vertical axis, the widest at the bottom and each one narrower than the one below, so the outline is a pyramid. Label from bottom: 'Producers (grasses)', 'Primary consumers (grasshoppers, herbivores)', 'Secondary consumers (lizards, birds)', 'Tertiary consumers (hawks, top carnivores)'. Beside each bar write a count per unit area that decreases sharply going up (NCERT's grassland figure uses values of the order of millions of producers, a few lakh herbivores and carnivores, and a handful of top carnivores). Write 'number of individuals per unit area' under the base and title the figure 'Pyramid of numbers, grassland, upright'.

diagrams.title: Pyramid of biomass in a grassland or forest (upright) beside pyramid of biomass in the sea (inverted)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two pyramids side by side. Left: four bars getting narrower upward, labelled producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers, tertiary consumers, unit 'dry weight, g m<sup>−2</sup>', title 'Pyramid of biomass, grassland or forest, upright'. Right: bars getting wider upward, the narrow base labelled 'phytoplankton (producers)', the wider bars above labelled 'zooplankton (primary consumers)' and 'fishes (secondary and tertiary consumers)', title 'Pyramid of biomass, sea, inverted'. Write the one-line reason under the right one: 'biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton'. The 2010 and 2013 questions ask for exactly this pair.

diagrams.title: Pyramid of numbers on a single tree (inverted)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a narrow base bar labelled 'one tree (producer)', a wider bar above it labelled 'fruit-eating birds and caterpillars (primary consumers)', and a still wider bar labelled 'insects and lice living on them (secondary consumers)' if you draw three levels; or just tree, herbivorous insects and birds, and insectivorous birds. The outline widens going up. Write 'number per unit area' and title 'Pyramid of numbers, tree-dominated ecosystem, inverted'. Add the reason: a single large producer supports a very large number of consumers.

diagrams.title: Pyramid of energy (always upright)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw four bars narrowing upward with energy values that fall by a factor of ten at each step, for example 10,000 kJ m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup> for producers, 1,000 for primary consumers, 100 for secondary consumers and 10 for tertiary consumers, and label each level. Between each pair of bars draw a small side arrow labelled 'energy lost as heat'. Write the unit kJ m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup> under the base and the caption 'pyramid of energy is always upright; can never be inverted because energy is lost as heat at each transfer'. Marks go to the labels, the tenfold decrease and the heat-loss arrows.

diagrams.title: Steps of decomposition (flow diagram)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Start with a box 'Detritus (dead leaves, bark, flowers, animal remains, faecal matter)'. Draw three arrows from it, side by side, to 'Fragmentation (by detritivores, e.g. earthworm)', 'Leaching (water-soluble nutrients precipitate in soil as unavailable salts)' and 'Catabolism (bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus)', with a bracket saying 'operate simultaneously'. From these draw an arrow to 'Humification: humus, dark, amorphous, colloidal, resistant, nutrient reservoir' and then to 'Mineralisation: release of inorganic nutrients (CO<sub>2</sub>, water, minerals)'. Add a side note: 'rate is faster when warm, moist, aerobic, detritus rich in nitrogen and sugars; slower when cold, anaerobic, rich in lignin and chitin'.

diagrams.title: The pond as a self-sustaining ecosystem
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a cross-section of a pond. Label the abiotic component: 'water with dissolved inorganic and organic substances' and 'rich soil deposit at the bottom'; draw the sun above with 'solar input, temperature cycle, day length'. Label producers: phytoplankton in the water, submerged plants, floating plants and marginal plants at the edge. Label consumers: zooplankton, free-swimming fish, bottom-dwelling forms. Label decomposers at the bottom: fungi, bacteria, flagellates. Around the drawing write the four functions as numbered arrows: inorganic to organic by autotrophs; consumption by heterotrophs; decomposition and mineralisation; unidirectional energy flow with heat loss.

ncert_questions.q: Fill in the blanks. (a) Plants are called as ______ because they fix carbon dioxide. (b) In an ecosystem dominated by trees, the pyramid (of numbers) is ______ type. (c) In aquatic ecosystems, the limiting factor for the productivity is ______. (d) Common detritivores in our ecosystem are ______.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Producers (autotrophs): they fix carbon dioxide into organic matter by photosynthesis.
(b) Inverted: a single tree supports a very large number of herbivorous insects and birds, so the number of consumers is greater than the number of producers.
(c) Light: sunlight penetrates only the upper layers of water, so photosynthesis and hence productivity fall with depth (some keys also accept nutrients, which limit productivity in the open ocean).
(d) Earthworms (also termites, millipedes and other small soil animals that fragment detritus).

NCERT's original part (e), 'the major reservoir of carbon on earth', belonged to the Nutrient Cycling section, which is deleted from the rationalised syllabus; it is not asked in the board paper.

ncert_questions.q: Which one of the following has the largest population in a food chain? (a) Producers (b) Primary consumers (c) Secondary consumers (d) Decomposers
ncert_questions.a: (d) Decomposers. Bacteria and fungi are present in enormous numbers at every trophic level because they act on the dead remains and wastes of producers and of all consumers. Their population is larger than that of the producers, which form the largest population within the grazing part of the chain.

ncert_questions.q: The second trophic level in a lake is (a) Phytoplankton (b) Zooplankton (c) Benthos (d) Fishes
ncert_questions.a: (b) Zooplankton. In a lake the food chain is Phytoplankton → Zooplankton → Fish. Phytoplankton are the producers (first trophic level); zooplankton feed on them and are the primary consumers, the second trophic level; fishes are secondary consumers.

ncert_questions.q: Secondary producers are (a) Herbivores (b) Producers (c) Carnivores (d) None of the above
ncert_questions.a: (a) Herbivores. Herbivores (primary consumers) convert the organic matter made by plants into new organic matter of their own body, which is called secondary production, so they are sometimes called secondary producers. Green plants are the primary producers.

ncert_questions.q: What is the percentage of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) in the incident solar radiation? (a) 100 per cent (b) 50 per cent (c) 1 to 5 per cent (d) 2 to 10 per cent
ncert_questions.a: (b) 50 per cent. NCERT states that of the incident solar radiation, less than 50 per cent is photosynthetically active radiation. The option 2 to 10 per cent is the fraction of PAR that plants actually capture, not the PAR fraction of sunlight; that is the trap in this question.

ncert_questions.q: Distinguish between grazing food chain and detritus food chain.
ncert_questions.a:
Grazing food chain (GFC): begins with living green plants (producers) that are eaten by herbivores, which are eaten by carnivores; e.g. Grass → Goat → Man, Phytoplankton → Zooplankton → Fish. Energy enters from the sun through photosynthesis. It is the major conduit of energy flow in aquatic ecosystems.
Detritus food chain (DFC): begins with dead organic matter (detritus) and is made up of decomposers, mainly fungi and bacteria (saprotrophs), that obtain energy and nutrients by degrading detritus. In terrestrial ecosystems a much larger fraction of energy flows through the DFC than through the GFC. The two chains are connected because DFC organisms are prey to GFC animals.

Production: the synthesis of organic matter from inorganic materials by producers (autotrophs) using solar energy, in photosynthesis. It builds biomass, stores energy and needs light and chlorophyll. Expressed as primary production (g m−2) and its rate as productivity.
Decomposition: the breakdown of complex dead organic matter (detritus) into inorganic substances such as CO2, water and nutrients by decomposers (bacteria, fungi) and detritivores. It releases energy as heat, returns nutrients to the pool, needs oxygen and is faster in warm, moist conditions. Production is the opposite of decomposition in the direction of matter and energy.

ncert_questions.q: Distinguish between upright and inverted pyramid.
ncert_questions.a:
Upright pyramid: the quantity (number, biomass or energy) decreases from the producers at the base to the top consumers at the apex, so the base is the widest bar. Examples: pyramid of numbers and of biomass in a grassland; pyramid of energy in every ecosystem.
Inverted pyramid: the quantity at a higher trophic level is greater than at the level below, so the base is the narrowest bar. Examples: pyramid of biomass in the sea (biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton) and pyramid of numbers in a tree-dominated ecosystem (one tree supports many insects and birds). The pyramid of energy can never be inverted.

ncert_questions.q: Distinguish between food chain and food web.
ncert_questions.a:
Food chain: a single linear sequence of organisms in which each is eaten by the next, showing one path of energy flow, e.g. Grass → Goat → Man. Each organism is shown at one trophic level.
Food web: a network of many interconnected food chains in a natural ecosystem, formed because most organisms eat and are eaten by more than one species (omnivores such as crows and cockroaches, and DFC organisms being prey to GFC animals). It shows the actual, branched pattern of energy flow and gives the ecosystem stability.

Litter: the dead plant material such as fallen leaves, twigs, bark and flowers lying on the surface of the soil (above ground).
Detritus: all the dead organic matter, above and below the ground, including the dead remains of plants and animals and faecal matter; it is the raw material for decomposition. Litter is therefore a part of detritus.

ncert_questions.q: Distinguish between primary and secondary productivity.
ncert_questions.a:
Primary productivity: the rate at which producers (green plants) make organic matter or biomass per unit area per unit time during photosynthesis, expressed in g m−2 yr−1 or kcal m−2 yr−1. It is divided into gross (GPP) and net (NPP = GPP − R).
Secondary productivity: the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers (heterotrophs) from the food they take in. It depends on the primary productivity and is always smaller than it.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the components of an ecosystem.
ncert_questions.a:
An ecosystem has two components, abiotic and biotic, and their interaction gives it a physical structure described by species composition and stratification.

Abiotic components: the non-living physical and chemical factors: sunlight, temperature, day length, water and climatic conditions; the inorganic substances (water, CO2, O2, minerals) and organic substances (dead matter, humus) in the soil or water. In a pond these are the water with dissolved substances and the rich soil deposit at the bottom, with solar input and temperature regulating the rate of functioning.

Biotic components, by their role in the food chain:

  1. Producers (autotrophs): green plants and photosynthetic bacteria that fix solar energy and make organic matter from inorganic materials. In a pond: phytoplankton, algae, and the floating, submerged and marginal plants.
  2. Consumers (heterotrophs): animals that depend on producers directly or indirectly. Primary consumers (herbivores, e.g. zooplankton), secondary consumers (primary carnivores, e.g. small fish) and tertiary consumers (secondary carnivores, e.g. large fish), including free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms.
  3. Decomposers (saprotrophs): fungi, bacteria and flagellates, abundant at the bottom, that break dead organic matter into inorganic substances and return nutrients for reuse by the autotrophs.

Together the components carry out the four functions: productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling.

ncert_questions.q: Define ecological pyramids and describe with examples pyramids of number and biomass.
ncert_questions.a:
An ecological pyramid is the graphic representation of the relationship between the different trophic levels of an ecosystem, in which the base represents the producers (first trophic level) and the apex represents the top-level consumers. The relationship may be expressed in terms of number, biomass or energy.

Pyramid of numbers: represents the number of individuals at each trophic level per unit area. In a grassland it is upright: a very large number of grass plants support fewer herbivores (grasshoppers), fewer carnivores (lizards, birds) and only a few top carnivores (hawks). In a tree-dominated ecosystem it is inverted: a single tree supports a large number of fruit-eating birds and a still larger number of insects.

Pyramid of biomass: represents the total dry weight of living matter (standing crop) at each trophic level per unit area. In a grassland or forest it is upright, because the biomass of producers exceeds that of herbivores, which exceeds that of carnivores. In the sea it is generally inverted, because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton: the phytoplankton have a small standing crop but reproduce very rapidly and are consumed as fast as they are produced.

(Draw the upright grassland pyramids and the inverted sea pyramid, labelling the four trophic levels and the unit.)

ncert_questions.q: What is primary productivity? Give a brief description of the factors that affect primary productivity.
ncert_questions.a:
Primary productivity is the rate at which biomass or organic matter is produced per unit area per unit time by plants during photosynthesis, expressed in g m−2 yr−1 or kcal m−2 yr−1. It has two parts: gross primary productivity (GPP), the total rate of organic matter production in photosynthesis, and net primary productivity (NPP), the part left after the plants' respiration losses (GPP − R = NPP), which is the biomass available to herbivores and decomposers.

Factors that affect primary productivity:

  1. Plant species inhabiting the area: different species have different growth rates and photosynthetic efficiencies.
  2. Environmental factors: sunlight, temperature and water; light limits productivity in deep water and in shaded places, low temperature and drought reduce it, which is why tropical rain forests are the most productive and deserts and deep oceans the least.
  3. Availability of nutrients: nitrogen, phosphorus and other minerals in the soil or water; the open ocean is nutrient-poor and so produces only 55 billion tons a year despite covering 70 per cent of the surface.
  4. Photosynthetic capacity of the plants: the efficiency with which the plants capture PAR (only 2 to 10 per cent) and convert it to biomass.

Because of these variations the annual NPP of the whole biosphere is about 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter, unevenly distributed among ecosystems.

ncert_questions.q: Define decomposition and describe the processes and products of decomposition.
ncert_questions.a:
Decomposition is the process by which decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like carbon dioxide, water and nutrients. The raw material is detritus: dead plant remains such as leaves, bark and flowers, and dead remains of animals including faecal matter.

Processes (steps):

  1. Fragmentation: detritivores such as earthworms break the detritus into smaller particles.
  2. Leaching: water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and are precipitated as unavailable salts.
  3. Catabolism: bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade the detritus into simpler inorganic substances. Fragmentation, leaching and catabolism operate simultaneously.
  4. Humification: accumulation of humus, a dark coloured amorphous substance highly resistant to microbial action, decomposing at an extremely slow rate; being colloidal it acts as a reservoir of nutrients.
  5. Mineralisation: humus is further degraded by some microbes and inorganic nutrients are released.

Products: carbon dioxide, water, heat, humus, and inorganic nutrients (minerals) that are returned to the soil for reuse by producers.

Factors: decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process. It is slower when detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, faster when rich in nitrogen and water-soluble sugars. Warm and moist conditions favour it; low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it, causing build-up of organic matter.

ncert_questions.q: Give an account of energy flow in an ecosystem.
ncert_questions.a:
Except for the deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystem, the sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems. Of the incident solar radiation, less than 50 per cent is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), and plants and photosynthetic bacteria capture only 2 to 10 per cent of the PAR; this small amount of energy sustains the entire living world.

Energy flow is unidirectional: from the sun to the producers and then to the consumers. Producers (first trophic level) fix solar energy in organic matter. Herbivores (primary consumers, second level) eat the producers; primary carnivores (secondary consumers, third level) eat the herbivores; secondary carnivores (tertiary consumers) eat them. This is the grazing food chain, e.g. Grass → Goat → Man. Dead remains and wastes of all levels form detritus, whose energy passes through the detritus food chain of decomposers (fungi and bacteria). In water the GFC is the major conduit of energy; on land a much larger fraction flows through the DFC.

Ecosystems obey the laws of thermodynamics: energy is only converted from one form to another, and at each transfer part of it is lost as heat. Transfer between trophic levels follows the 10 per cent law: only about 10 per cent of the energy of a trophic level is passed to the next; with 10,000 units in the producers, herbivores get about 1,000, primary carnivores 100 and secondary carnivores 10. This is why the number of trophic levels is restricted to four or five and why the pyramid of energy is always upright. Since energy is dissipated as heat at every level and never returns, an ecosystem needs a constant input of solar energy.

(Draw the energy-flow diagram: sun → producers → primary → secondary → tertiary consumers, arrows from all levels to decomposers, heat lost at every step.)

pyq.q: Which one of the following ecological pyramids can never be inverted?
options: Pyramid of biomass in the sea
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Some energy is always lost as heat at each transfer between trophic levels, so the energy at a lower level is always greater than at the level above; the pyramid of energy is therefore always upright.

pyq.q: Of the incident solar radiation, the fraction that is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) is:
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: NCERT: less than 50 per cent of incident solar radiation is PAR. The 2 to 10 per cent figure is the fraction of PAR that plants capture.

pyq.q: The pyramid of biomass is generally inverted in:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: In the sea the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of the phytoplankton producers, which have a small standing crop but a very fast turnover, so the pyramid of biomass is inverted.

pyq.q: The dark coloured, amorphous, colloidal substance that accumulates during decomposition and is highly resistant to microbial action is:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Humification produces humus, which decomposes at an extremely slow rate and, being colloidal, serves as a reservoir of nutrients.

pyq.q: In a terrestrial ecosystem, a much larger fraction of energy flows through the:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: On land most of the primary production is not eaten alive but dies and becomes detritus, so the detritus food chain carries the larger fraction; in aquatic ecosystems the grazing food chain is the major conduit.

pyq.q: The annual net primary productivity of the whole biosphere is approximately:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: NCERT gives about 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter per year for the biosphere, of which the oceans contribute only 55 billion tons despite covering about 70 per cent of the surface.

pyq.q: Which of the following statements about decomposition is correct?
options: It is faster when detritus is rich in lignin and chitin
It is inhibited by warm and moist conditions
It is largely an oxygen-requiring process
Leaching precipitates nutrients as readily available salts
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Decomposition is largely aerobic. Lignin and chitin slow it, warm and moist conditions favour it, and leaching precipitates nutrients as unavailable salts.

pyq.q: A sparrow that eats seeds and peas and also insects and worms is an example showing that:
options: A trophic level is a functional level, not a species
Decomposers occupy the second trophic level
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The sparrow is a primary consumer when it eats seeds and a secondary consumer when it eats insects, so one species can occupy more than one trophic level; a trophic level is defined by the source of food, not by the species.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The pyramid of energy is always upright. Reason (R): When energy flows from one trophic level to the next, some energy is always lost as heat.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Heat loss at every transfer means the energy at a lower level is always more than at the next, so the energy pyramid can never be inverted; R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The pyramid of biomass in the sea is generally inverted. Reason (R): The biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: This is NCERT's own reason for the inverted marine biomass pyramid: a small, fast-turning-over standing crop of phytoplankton supports a much larger biomass of consumers.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Decomposition is slower when detritus is rich in lignin and chitin. Reason (R): Lignin and chitin are readily attacked by bacterial and fungal enzymes.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: A is NCERT's statement. R is false: lignin and chitin resist microbial enzymes, which is exactly why detritus rich in them decomposes slowly, while nitrogen and sugars speed decomposition.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): In a terrestrial ecosystem a much larger fraction of energy flows through the detritus food chain than through the grazing food chain. Reason (R): The detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Both statements are true NCERT lines, but R only defines the DFC; the reason a larger fraction flows through it on land is that most plant production dies uneaten and becomes detritus rather than being grazed.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Net primary productivity, not gross primary productivity, is the biomass available to herbivores and decomposers. Reason (R): A considerable part of the gross primary productivity is used by the plants themselves in respiration.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: GPP − R = NPP; what the plant respires away is never available to consumers, so only NPP is available and R is the correct explanation.

pyq.q: How does a detritivore differ from a decomposer? Explain with an example of each.
pyq.answer:
A detritivore is an animal that feeds on detritus and breaks it down into smaller particles by physical fragmentation; the nutrients are absorbed after the food is digested inside its body. Example: earthworm.
A decomposer is a microorganism that secretes digestive enzymes on to the detritus, degrades it chemically (catabolism) into simple inorganic substances outside its body and then absorbs them; it is a saprotroph. Examples: bacteria and fungi.
(Marking: one point of difference in mode of action, one example each.)

pyq.q: How is stratification represented in a forest ecosystem?
pyq.answer: Stratification is the vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels of an ecosystem. In a forest it is represented by distinct layers: trees occupy the top vertical strata or layer, shrubs the second, and herbs and grasses occupy the bottom layer. Stratification is one of the two features (with species composition) that describe the physical structure of the ecosystem.

pyq.q: What does R represent in the equation for productivity, GPP − R = NPP? Mention any two reasons why primary productivity varies in different types of ecosystems.
pyq.answer:
R represents the respiration losses of the plants: the considerable part of the gross primary productivity that the plants use up in their own respiration; subtracting it gives the net primary productivity available to heterotrophs.
Primary productivity varies because it depends on (any two): (i) the plant species inhabiting the area; (ii) environmental factors such as light, temperature and water; (iii) the availability of nutrients; (iv) the photosynthetic capacity of the plants.

pyq.q: State what the standing crop of a trophic level represents. List two ways of measuring it.
pyq.answer:
The standing crop of a trophic level is the mass of living material present at that trophic level at a particular time.
It is measured (i) as the biomass of the living organisms per unit area, expressed as fresh weight or, more accurately, dry weight; or (ii) as the number of individuals per unit area.

pyq.q: Why are green algae not likely to be found in the deepest strata of the ocean? What is a detritus food chain made up of?
pyq.answer:
Green algae are photosynthetic producers and need light; sunlight (PAR) cannot penetrate to the deepest strata of the ocean, so photosynthesis is impossible there and green algae cannot survive. Light is the limiting factor for productivity in aquatic ecosystems.
A detritus food chain is made up of decomposers, heterotrophic organisms that are mainly fungi and bacteria (saprotrophs), which meet their energy and nutrient needs by degrading dead organic matter (detritus).

pyq.q: Define humification and mineralisation. Why is the earthworm called the farmer's friend?
pyq.answer:
Humification is the step of decomposition that leads to the accumulation of humus, a dark coloured amorphous, colloidal substance that is highly resistant to microbial action, decomposes extremely slowly and serves as a reservoir of nutrients.
Mineralisation is the further degradation of humus by some microbes with the release of inorganic nutrients into the soil.
The earthworm is the farmer's friend because it fragments complex organic matter (detritus) into smaller particles, speeding decomposition and nutrient release, and its burrowing loosens and aerates the soil.

pyq.q: Name the type of food chain responsible for the flow of a larger fraction of energy in a terrestrial ecosystem and in an aquatic ecosystem. Give one example of a grazing food chain from each.
pyq.answer:
In a terrestrial ecosystem a much larger fraction of energy flows through the detritus food chain; in an aquatic ecosystem the grazing food chain is the major conduit for energy flow.
Grazing food chain examples: terrestrial, Grass → Goat → Man; aquatic, Phytoplankton → Zooplankton → Fish.

pyq.q: Write the relationship between productivity, gross primary productivity, net primary productivity and secondary productivity.
pyq.answer:
Productivity is the rate of production of biomass per unit area per unit time (g m−2 yr−1 or kcal m−2 yr−1). It is of two kinds, primary (by producers) and secondary (by consumers).
Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total rate of production of organic matter by plants during photosynthesis. A considerable part of it is used by the plants in respiration (R).
Net primary productivity (NPP) is what remains after respiration: GPP − R = NPP. NPP is the biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers).
Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers; it is built from the NPP they consume and is therefore always smaller than NPP.
So: productivity is divided into primary and secondary; primary into gross and net; NPP feeds secondary productivity.

pyq.q: Describe how oxygen and the chemical composition of detritus control decomposition.
pyq.answer:
Oxygen: decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring (aerobic) process, because the decomposer bacteria and fungi respire aerobically while degrading detritus. Anaerobiosis (lack of oxygen, as in waterlogged soil) inhibits decomposition and leads to a build-up of undecomposed organic matter.
Chemical composition of detritus: in a given climate, decomposition is slower when the detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, which resist microbial enzymes, and quicker when it is rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars, which microbes use readily.
Climate (if asked): temperature and soil moisture regulate decomposition through their effect on soil microbes; warm and moist conditions favour it, low temperature inhibits it.

pyq.q: Why is the pyramid of energy always upright? Explain with a labelled diagram.
pyq.answer:
The pyramid of energy shows the energy content (kJ m−2 yr−1) at each trophic level, producers at the base and top carnivores at the apex.
When energy flows from one trophic level to the next, some energy is always lost as heat at each step (Second law of thermodynamics), and part is used in the metabolism of the organisms of that level. Only about 10 per cent of the energy is transferred (10 per cent law). So the energy at a lower trophic level is always greater than at the level above it: e.g. 10,000 units in producers, 1,000 in herbivores, 100 in primary carnivores, 10 in secondary carnivores. The bars must get shorter going up; the pyramid can never be inverted.
Diagram: four bars narrowing upward labelled producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers, tertiary consumers with values 10,000, 1,000, 100, 10 kJ m−2 yr−1, and side arrows marked 'heat loss' between levels.

pyq.q: 'In a food chain, a trophic level represents a functional level, not a species.' Explain with an example.
pyq.answer:
A trophic level is the place an organism occupies in a food chain based on the source of its food, not on which species it is: producers form the first level, herbivores the second, carnivores the third.
A single species can therefore occupy more than one trophic level at the same time, depending on what it eats. A sparrow is a primary consumer (second trophic level) when it eats seeds, fruits and peas, but a secondary consumer (third trophic level) when it eats insects and worms. Likewise a human eating rice is a primary consumer and eating fish is a secondary or tertiary consumer.
Since the level is decided by the function performed (what is eaten) rather than by the species, a trophic level is a functional level, not a species as such. This is also one of the limitations of ecological pyramids, which cannot show a species at two levels.

pyq.q: Draw the pyramids of biomass in a sea and in a forest. Explain the shape of each.
pyq.answer:
Forest: upright pyramid of biomass. Draw four bars narrowing upward: producers (trees, largest dry weight per m2), primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers, tertiary consumers. The biomass of producers exceeds that of herbivores, which exceeds that of carnivores, because only about 10 per cent of the energy, and hence a small fraction of the biomass, is passed to each higher level.
Sea: inverted pyramid of biomass. Draw a narrow base of phytoplankton (producers), a wider bar of zooplankton (primary consumers) and the widest bar of fishes (secondary and tertiary consumers). The biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton because the phytoplankton have a small standing crop at any moment but reproduce very fast and are eaten almost as quickly as they are produced, so a small producer biomass supports a much larger consumer biomass.
Label the trophic levels and the unit (dry weight, g m−2) on both.

pyq.q: Taking the example of a small pond, explain how the four components of an ecosystem function as a unit.
pyq.answer:
A pond is a small, shallow, self-sustainable ecosystem with four components:
(i) Abiotic: the water with dissolved inorganic and organic substances and the rich soil deposit at the bottom; solar input, temperature cycle and day length regulate the rate of functioning.
(ii) Producers (autotrophs): phytoplankton, some algae, and floating, submerged and marginal plants.
(iii) Consumers: zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms.
(iv) Decomposers: fungi, bacteria and flagellates, abundant at the bottom.
They function as a unit by performing all the functions of an ecosystem: (1) conversion of inorganic into organic material by the autotrophs using the sun's radiant energy; (2) consumption of the autotrophs by the heterotrophs; (3) decomposition and mineralisation of dead matter, releasing nutrients back for reuse by the autotrophs; (4) unidirectional movement of energy towards higher trophic levels and its dissipation and loss as heat.

pyq.q: List the steps of decomposition in order and write one sentence on each. Which of them operate simultaneously?
pyq.answer:
(1) Fragmentation: detritivores such as earthworms break detritus into smaller particles.
(2) Leaching: water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and are precipitated as unavailable salts.
(3) Catabolism: bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances.
(4) Humification: accumulation of humus, a dark coloured amorphous colloidal substance resistant to microbial action, which acts as a nutrient reservoir.
(5) Mineralisation: humus is further degraded by some microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients.
Fragmentation, leaching and catabolism operate simultaneously on the detritus.

pyq.q: What are the limitations of ecological pyramids?
pyq.answer:
(1) Ecological pyramids do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels (for example a sparrow that is both a primary and a secondary consumer); each species is placed at one level only.
(2) They assume a simple food chain, something that almost never exists in nature; they do not accommodate a food web, in which organisms are linked to many others.
(3) Saprophytes (decomposers) are not given any place in ecological pyramids, even though they play a vital role in the ecosystem by recycling nutrients and carrying a large share of the energy flow on land.
(Any additional point: they do not show seasonal changes in standing crop or the rate of turnover, which is why the biomass pyramid of the sea looks inverted.)

pyq.q: Give an account of energy flow in an ecosystem with the help of a labelled diagram. State the law that governs the transfer of energy between trophic levels.
pyq.answer:
Source: except for the deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystem, the sun is the only source of energy. Less than 50 per cent of incident solar radiation is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR); plants and photosynthetic bacteria capture only 2 to 10 per cent of the PAR, and this sustains the entire living world.
Unidirectional flow: energy flows from the sun to the producers (first trophic level), from producers to primary consumers (herbivores), then to secondary consumers (primary carnivores) and tertiary consumers (secondary carnivores). It never returns to the sun or to a lower level.
Two food chains: the grazing food chain starts with living plants (Grass → Goat → Man; Phytoplankton → Zooplankton → Fish); the detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter and consists of decomposers (fungi and bacteria, saprotrophs). The GFC dominates energy flow in water; on land a much larger fraction flows through the DFC. The two are connected into a food web.
Laws: ecosystems obey the First law (energy is converted, not created or destroyed) and the Second law (some energy is degraded to heat at every transfer) of thermodynamics; hence they need a constant supply of energy.
10 per cent law: only about 10 per cent of the energy of one trophic level is transferred to the next; the rest is used in metabolism, lost as heat or passes to detritus. With 10,000 units in producers, herbivores receive 1,000, primary carnivores 100 and secondary carnivores 10. This restricts food chains to four or five levels and makes the pyramid of energy always upright.
Diagram: sun → producers → primary consumers → secondary consumers → tertiary consumers in a line with decreasing values; arrows from every level to a decomposer box; wavy 'heat loss' arrows from every box.

pyq.q: Define an ecological pyramid. Describe the pyramids of number, biomass and energy with labelled diagrams, giving one example of an inverted pyramid of each type where it exists, and state their limitations.
pyq.answer:
Definition: an ecological pyramid is the graphic representation of the relationship between different trophic levels of an ecosystem in terms of number, biomass or energy, with the producers at the base and the top-level consumers at the apex.
Pyramid of numbers: number of individuals per unit area at each level. Upright in a grassland (many grass plants, fewer grasshoppers, fewer lizards, a few hawks). Inverted in a tree-dominated ecosystem, where one tree supports many birds and a larger number of insects.
Pyramid of biomass: dry weight of living matter (standing crop) per unit area at each level. Upright in grasslands and forests, since producers outweigh herbivores, which outweigh carnivores. Inverted in the sea, because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton, which have a small but rapidly renewed standing crop.
Pyramid of energy: energy content (kJ m−2 yr−1) at each level. Always upright, e.g. 10,000, 1,000, 100, 10, because some energy is lost as heat at each transfer (10 per cent law); it can never be inverted.
Limitations: (i) they do not account for a species occupying two or more trophic levels; (ii) they assume a simple food chain, which almost never exists, and cannot accommodate a food web; (iii) saprophytes (decomposers) are given no place although they play a vital role.
Diagrams: draw the upright grassland pyramids of number and biomass, the inverted sea pyramid of biomass, and the upright energy pyramid, each with four labelled trophic levels and the unit.

pyq.q: Define decomposition. Describe the processes and products of decomposition and explain the factors that affect its rate.
pyq.answer:
Decomposition is the breakdown of complex organic matter by decomposers into inorganic substances like carbon dioxide, water and nutrients. Its raw material is detritus: dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) and dead animal remains including faecal matter.
Processes: (1) Fragmentation: detritivores (earthworms) break detritus into smaller particles. (2) Leaching: water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and precipitate as unavailable salts. (3) Catabolism: bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances. These three operate simultaneously. (4) Humification: accumulation of humus, a dark, amorphous, colloidal substance highly resistant to microbial action that decomposes extremely slowly and acts as a reservoir of nutrients. (5) Mineralisation: humus is further degraded by some microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients.
Products: carbon dioxide, water, heat, humus and mineral nutrients returned to the soil for producers.
Factors affecting rate: (i) Oxygen: decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process; anaerobiosis inhibits it. (ii) Chemical composition of detritus: slower when rich in lignin and chitin, quicker when rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars. (iii) Climate: temperature and soil moisture regulate it through the activity of soil microbes; warm and moist conditions favour decomposition, low temperature inhibits it, causing a build-up of organic material.
Draw the flow diagram detritus → fragmentation, leaching, catabolism (simultaneous) → humification → mineralisation.

pyq.q: Describe the structure of an ecosystem and explain, with the pond as an example, the four functional aspects that make it a functional unit.
pyq.answer:
Structure: an ecosystem is a functional unit of nature in which organisms interact among themselves and with the physical environment. The interaction of its biotic and abiotic components gives it a physical structure described by (i) species composition, the identification and enumeration of plant and animal species, and (ii) stratification, the vertical distribution of species at different levels (in a forest, trees at the top, shrubs second, herbs and grasses at the bottom).
Components of a pond: abiotic (water with dissolved inorganic and organic substances, the rich soil deposit at the bottom, solar input, temperature and day length); producers (phytoplankton, algae, floating, submerged and marginal plants); consumers (zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms); decomposers (fungi, bacteria and flagellates at the bottom).
Four functional aspects: (1) Productivity: autotrophs convert inorganic materials to organic matter using the sun's radiant energy; the rate is GPP, and GPP − R = NPP is what heterotrophs can use. (2) Decomposition: dead matter is broken down and mineralised by decomposers (fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, mineralisation), releasing nutrients for reuse by autotrophs. (3) Energy flow: unidirectional movement of energy from the sun through producers to consumers, with about 10 per cent transferred at each level and the rest dissipated as heat. (4) Nutrient cycling: the minerals released by decomposition are taken up again by producers, so matter circulates while energy passes through.
Because it carries out all four, the pond, like the biosphere, is a self-sustaining functional unit.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A student measured productivity in two ecosystems over one year. In a grassland the gross primary productivity was 2,400 g m−2 yr−1 and the plants respired 900 g m−2 yr−1. In a nearby lake the gross primary productivity was 800 g m−2 yr−1 and respiration was 350 g m−2 yr−1. She also noted that the herbivores of the grassland built 120 g m−2 yr−1 of new tissue.
(i) Calculate the net primary productivity of each ecosystem.
(ii) What name is given to the 120 g m−2 yr−1 figure? Define it.
(iii) Give two reasons why the lake's productivity is lower than the grassland's.
(iv) Why is NPP, and not GPP, the quantity available to the herbivores?
pyq.answer:
(i) NPP = GPP − R. Grassland: 2,400 − 900 = 1,500 g m−2 yr−1. Lake: 800 − 350 = 450 g m−2 yr−1.
(ii) It is the secondary productivity: the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.
(iii) Any two: light is the limiting factor in water and penetrates only the upper layers; nutrients are less available in the water column; the plant species (phytoplankton) have a smaller standing crop and different photosynthetic capacity; temperature of the water differs from that of the land.
(iv) A considerable part of the GPP is used up by the plants themselves in respiration (R) and is lost as heat; only what remains as plant biomass, the NPP, can be eaten by herbivores or used by decomposers.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. Two pyramids were drawn from a grassland and from the open sea. In the grassland the producers had a standing crop of about 800 g m−2, the herbivores about 40 g m−2 and the carnivores about 10 g m−2. In the sea the phytoplankton had a standing crop of only a few grams per square metre, while the zooplankton and fishes together weighed several times more. A third pyramid drawn for the energy content of the grassland showed 10,000, 1,000, 100 and 10 kJ m−2 yr−1 at the four trophic levels.
(i) Name the type of pyramid drawn for the grassland and the sea, and state the shape of each.
(ii) Why is the sea pyramid shaped that way?
(iii) What law is illustrated by the energy pyramid figures? State it.
(iv) Give one limitation of such pyramids.
pyq.answer:
(i) Both are pyramids of biomass (standing crop in g m−2). The grassland pyramid is upright (800 → 40 → 10 decreases going up); the sea pyramid is inverted (a narrow base of phytoplankton below wider consumer bars).
(ii) The biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton; the phytoplankton have a small standing crop at any instant but multiply very rapidly and are eaten as fast as they are produced, so a small producer biomass supports a much larger consumer biomass.
(iii) The 10 per cent law: only about 10 per cent of the energy of a trophic level is transferred to the next; the rest is used in metabolism and lost as heat. 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 is a tenfold fall at each step, so the energy pyramid is always upright.
(iv) Any one: they do not account for a species belonging to two or more trophic levels; they assume a simple food chain and cannot show a food web; saprophytes (decomposers) are given no place.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a man-made ecosystem?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT lists crop fields and an aquarium as man-made ecosystems; estuary, wetland and grassland are natural.

practice_mcq.q: The vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels in an ecosystem is called:
practice_mcq.explanation: Stratification: in a forest, trees occupy the top layer, shrubs the second, and herbs and grasses the bottom.

practice_mcq.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four functional aspects of an ecosystem named by NCERT?
practice_mcq.explanation: The four functional aspects are productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling; stratification describes structure, not function.

practice_mcq.q: Primary production is expressed in units of:
practice_mcq.explanation: Production is an amount per unit area (g m<sup>−2</sup> or kcal m<sup>−2</sup>); productivity is its rate, per unit time (g m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup>).

practice_mcq.q: If the GPP of an ecosystem is 3,600 kcal m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup> and NPP is 2,100 kcal m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup>, the respiratory loss R is:
practice_mcq.explanation: GPP − R = NPP, so R = GPP − NPP = 3,600 − 2,100 = 1,500 kcal m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup>.

practice_mcq.q: Despite occupying about 70 per cent of the Earth's surface, the oceans contribute an annual NPP of only:
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: 170 billion tons for the whole biosphere, of which the oceans give only 55 billion tons; the rest is from land.

practice_mcq.q: The rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers is called:
practice_mcq.explanation: Secondary productivity is defined as the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.

practice_mcq.q: Which step of decomposition results in water-soluble inorganic nutrients going down into the soil horizon and being precipitated as unavailable salts?
practice_mcq.explanation: Leaching is the downward movement of soluble nutrients into the soil, where they precipitate as unavailable salts.

practice_mcq.q: Which set of conditions gives the fastest decomposition?
options: Cold, waterlogged soil with detritus rich in lignin
Warm, moist, aerobic soil with detritus rich in nitrogen and sugars
Warm, dry soil with detritus rich in chitin
Cold, dry soil with detritus rich in sugars
practice_mcq.explanation: Decomposition needs oxygen and is favoured by warmth, moisture and detritus rich in nitrogen and water-soluble sugars; lignin, chitin, cold and anaerobiosis slow it.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is the raw material for decomposition?
practice_mcq.explanation: Detritus, the dead remains of plants and animals including faecal matter, is the raw material; humus, minerals and CO<sub>2</sub> are products.

practice_mcq.q: The only ecosystem on Earth that does not depend on the sun as its source of energy is the:
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: except for the deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystem, the sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems.

practice_mcq.q: Plants capture what fraction of the photosynthetically active radiation?
practice_mcq.explanation: PAR is less than 50 per cent of sunlight; plants capture only 2 to 10 per cent of that PAR, which sustains the entire living world.

practice_mcq.q: In the food chain Phytoplankton → Zooplankton → Fish, the fish is a:
practice_mcq.explanation: Phytoplankton are producers, zooplankton the primary consumers (herbivores), and the fish that eats zooplankton is a secondary consumer (primary carnivore).

practice_mcq.q: Decomposers are also called saprotrophs because they:
options: Obtain energy by degrading dead organic matter
practice_mcq.explanation: Sapro means to decompose; saprotrophs secrete enzymes on dead and waste material, break it into inorganic substances and absorb them.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following animals is named by NCERT as an omnivore that links the grazing and detritus food chains?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT names cockroaches and crows as omnivores whose feeding connects the DFC with the GFC, forming a food web.

practice_mcq.q: Measurement of standing crop in terms of dry weight rather than fresh weight is preferred because:
options: Dry weight is easier to obtain
Water content varies and dry weight is more accurate
Fresh weight cannot be measured for plants
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: biomass may be expressed as fresh or dry weight, and measurement in dry weight is more accurate, since the water content of organisms varies.

practice_mcq.q: In a pyramid of numbers drawn for a single large tree with the insects and birds it supports, the shape is:
practice_mcq.explanation: One producer supports a very large number of consumers, so the number rises going up the levels and the pyramid is inverted.

practice_mcq.q: If producers of a grassland contain 20,000 kJ m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup> of energy, the energy expected at the tertiary consumer level by the 10 per cent law is:
practice_mcq.explanation: Three transfers: producers 20,000 → primary consumers 2,000 → secondary consumers 200 → tertiary consumers 20 kJ m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup>.

practice_mcq.q: Which of these is a limitation of ecological pyramids?
options: They cannot be drawn for aquatic ecosystems
They give no place to saprophytes
practice_mcq.explanation: The three NCERT limitations: a species at more than one level is not accommodated, a simple food chain is assumed rather than a food web, and saprophytes are given no place.

practice_mcq.q: Humus serves as a reservoir of nutrients because it is:
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: humus is colloidal in nature and therefore serves as a reservoir of nutrients; it is amorphous, dark and resistant to microbial action.

common_mistakes: Confusing the two percentages in energy flow: less than 50 per cent of incident sunlight is PAR, and plants capture 2 to 10 per cent of that PAR. Writing '2 to 10 per cent of sunlight' or '50 per cent captured by plants' loses the mark, and NCERT exercise 5 is set precisely on this confusion.
Writing GPP + R = NPP or getting an NPP larger than GPP in a numerical. Respiration is subtracted: GPP − R = NPP, and NPP must always be smaller than GPP.

Calling the earthworm a decomposer. It is a detritivore that fragments detritus; decomposers are the bacteria and fungi that degrade it chemically with enzymes. The 2-mark 'detritivore versus decomposer' question tests exactly this.

Listing the five steps of decomposition out of order or as a strict sequence. Write fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, mineralisation, and add that the first three operate simultaneously.

Saying decomposition is faster when detritus is rich in lignin and chitin. It is the opposite: lignin and chitin slow decomposition; nitrogen and water-soluble sugars speed it up. Also remember that decomposition needs oxygen and is inhibited by anaerobiosis and low temperature.

Claiming the pyramid of energy can be inverted, or that the pyramid of biomass is inverted in a forest. Energy pyramids are always upright; the inverted cases are biomass in the sea and numbers on a tree.

Drawing pyramids without labels or units. Every bar must carry its trophic level (producers, primary, secondary, tertiary consumers) and the figure must state whether it shows number, biomass (g m<sup>−2</sup>) or energy (kJ m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup>); unlabelled diagrams score at most half.

Saying that in every ecosystem the grazing food chain carries most of the energy. That is true for aquatic ecosystems; in terrestrial ecosystems a much larger fraction flows through the detritus food chain.

Reviving deleted material: describing succession, the carbon or phosphorus cycle, or ecosystem services in a 5-mark answer on this chapter. They are no longer in the syllabus and earn nothing; spend the time on the diagram instead.

Defining an ecosystem as 'a place where organisms live'. NCERT's wording is a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and with the surrounding physical environment; both kinds of interaction are needed.
strategy:
This is the shortest chapter in the ecology unit after rationalisation and the most predictable, so prepare it for full marks rather than for coverage. Read the five NCERT sections once, slowly, underlining every definition, list and number: the definition of an ecosystem, species composition and stratification, the four functional aspects, GPP − R = NPP, the units, 170 and 55 billion tons, the five steps of decomposition and the factors that control it, less than 50 per cent and 2 to 10 per cent, the two NCERT food chains, the sparrow, standing crop, the 10 per cent law, the three pyramids with their exceptions and the three limitations. Those items are the entire question bank.

Then practise the diagrams from memory: the energy-flow diagram with the sun, four trophic levels, decomposers and heat loss; the four pyramids (numbers in a grassland, biomass in a grassland and in the sea, energy); and the decomposition flow chart. Draw each one twice on paper with full labels and units. A 5-mark question from this chapter is usually a definition plus a labelled diagram plus a short list, so the diagram is where the time goes.

Answer the eleven NCERT exercise questions in writing, especially the six 'distinguish between' pairs and the four long ones (components, pyramids, productivity factors, decomposition, energy flow). Skip anything in old papers on succession, nutrient cycles or ecosystem services; it is out of the syllabus. In the exam, budget about two minutes per mark, quote NCERT phrases word for word where you can ('functional level, not a species', 'largely an oxygen-requiring process', 'can never be inverted'), and always give the reason with the fact: not just 'inverted in the sea' but 'because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton'.
